Before diving into the many meanings, here is the thread that runs through all of them:

A token is something small — an object, a sign, or a piece of data — that stands in for, represents, or grants access to something larger or more abstract.

Think of it as a placeholder or a symbol. A token is never the main thing itself; it always points beyond itself to something else. This core idea will help you recognize the word no matter where you encounter it.
1. A Physical Object That Works Like Money (But Isn't)

This is the most familiar meaning. A token is a small physical object — usually a coin-shaped piece of metal or plastic — that you use instead of real currency within a specific, limited system.

A subway token is a small metal disc. You drop it into a turnstile, and the gate opens. The disc itself has almost no material value, but within that transit system, it is accepted as payment for a fare.

Other examples: arcade tokens (you exchange real money for them, then use them to play games), laundry tokens, bus tokens.

The key point: a token like this has no value outside its system. Inside the system, it substitutes for money and grants you access to something.
2. A Symbol or Sign of a Feeling

A token can be a small object or gesture that symbolizes something emotional — a feeling, a relationship, or a moment of significance.

"She gave him a token of her affection." She gave him something small — perhaps a locket, a handwritten note, a small gift — that represents her feelings.

"Please accept this as a token of our gratitude." Here, a small gift stands in for a much larger feeling of thankfulness.

The object given doesn't need to be expensive or grand. Its entire value lies in what it represents, not in what it physically is. The token is a tangible piece of something intangible.
3. Proof or Evidence of Something

A token can serve as a concrete piece of evidence — proof that you have a right, an identity, or a permission.

Historically, a messenger might carry a marked coin or a wax seal from a king to prove to strangers that they were authorized. That object was their token — their proof. In this sense, a token is similar to a ticket, a badge, a receipt, or a pass. It is something you can show to demonstrate that something is true.
4. A Voucher or Gift Card (Mainly British English)

In British English, a "token" commonly refers to what Americans call a gift card or voucher.

"I received a book token for my birthday." This means a voucher worth a specific amount that can be exchanged for books at a shop.

"Gift token" in British English = gift card in American English.
5. A Game Piece

In board games, the small movable objects that players use to represent themselves on the board are called tokens.

"Each player selects a token before the game begins." In a game like Monopoly, the little metal car, the hat, or the dog — those are tokens. They are stand-ins for the players themselves within the game world.
6. In Computing and Artificial Intelligence

This is one of the most important modern uses, and it is worth understanding carefully.

In computing, a token is the smallest individual unit that a system processes as a single, meaningful chunk.

When an AI language model reads text, it does not process it letter by letter, nor does it always split it neatly by spaces. It breaks the text into tokens using its own rules. A token might be:

  • A whole common word: "cat" → 1 token
  • Part of a longer or unusual word: "unbelievable" might become "un" + "believ" + "able" → 3 tokens
  • A punctuation mark: "." → 1 token
  • A number or symbol: "$" → 1 token

This is called tokenization — the process of breaking text into tokens before processing it.

Why does this matter? AI language models have a limit on how many tokens they can handle in one conversation, called a context window. When you hear that an AI can handle "128,000 tokens," it means roughly that many text chunks can fit into its active memory at once.

In programming, when a computer reads and interprets code, it also first breaks it into tokens: keywords like if or while, operators like + or =, and variable names. Each of these is a token — a recognized, meaningful unit.
7. In Blockchain and Cryptocurrency

In the world of digital currency and blockchain technology, a token is a digital unit that represents value, ownership, or rights within a specific system.

It helps to know the distinction between a coin and a token in this world:

  • A coin (like Bitcoin) runs on its own independent blockchain.
  • A token is built on top of an already-existing blockchain (like Ethereum).

Tokens can represent many things:

  • A unit of digital currency
  • Ownership of a digital asset
  • The right to access a service or platform
  • A share in a project or organization

The most well-known example is an NFT (Non-Fungible Token) — a unique digital token stored on a blockchain that proves ownership of a specific digital item, such as a piece of digital artwork. "Non-fungible" simply means it is one-of-a-kind and cannot be exchanged one-for-one with another token the way identical coins can.
8. In Security and Authentication

A security token or authentication token is something — physical or digital — that proves your identity and authorizes you to access something.

Physical security token: A small hardware device (like a USB key or a small fob) that stores or generates a code. When logging into a secure system, you might be required to plug this in or read its display code, proving you physically possess it.

Digital/software token: A string of data that a website or app stores to remember that you have already verified your identity. When you log into a website and stay logged in as you click from page to page, a token quietly tells the server "this person already proved who they are — let them through." This is why you don't have to re-enter your password on every single page.
9. In Linguistics and Philosophy (Type vs. Token)

This is a precise, technical distinction used in linguistics, logic, and philosophy.

Consider this sentence: "The cat sat on the mat."

The word the appears twice in that sentence.

Scholars in these fields draw a sharp line between two concepts:

  • Type: The abstract, general word "the" — there is only one type here.
  • Token: Each individual, concrete occurrence of that word in real text or speech. In this sentence, "the" has two tokens — two actual appearances.

A "type" is the category; a "token" is one specific, real-world instance of that category.

Practical example: A novel might contain 90,000 word tokens (that many words appear in total), but only around 12,000 unique word types (because countless words repeat). Every single "the," "and," "a" counts as a token each time it appears, but they each represent just one type.
The Phrase: "By the Same Token"

This is a very common English idiom. It means: for the same reason, using the same logic, or in the same way.

"You expect others to keep their promises; by the same token, you must keep yours."

The underlying idea comes from the sense of a token as proof or evidence: the same evidence that proves one thing also proves the related thing. If one argument holds, the parallel argument holds too.
Bringing It All Together

No matter the context you meet this word in, a token always shares this essential quality: it is something small that represents, substitutes for, or grants access to something larger.

  • A subway token represents a fare.
  • A token of love represents deep feeling.
  • A proof-token represents your identity or authorization.
  • A computing token represents a meaningful unit of text.
  • A blockchain token represents value or ownership.
  • A linguistic token represents one specific occurrence of a word.

The word always points past itself to something beyond. That is what makes "token" such a flexible word — the same logic of standing in for something bigger applies cleanly across every domain where it appears.
